commands.name: learn
commands.description: Learn the real-world idea behind the game. Try 'learn' alone for topics.

ip: An IP address identifies a machine on a network, like a street address.
10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x and 192.168.x.x are private ranges used inside companies and homes.
The game's public-looking IPs (192.0.2.x, 198.51.100.x, 203.0.113.x) are reserved for documentation, so they never belong to anyone real.
scan: Scanning finds which machines are alive and which ports they have open.
The real-world tool is nmap. Only scan networks you own or have written permission to test.
ports: A port is a numbered door on a machine. Each service listens on its own port.
Common ones: 21 FTP (file transfer), 22 SSH (remote shell), 80 HTTP (web), 443 HTTPS (secure web).
Every open port is a possible way in, so admins close the ones they don't need.
ssh: SSH (port 22) gives you a remote command line on a machine.
Well-run servers block password guessing on SSH, so attackers look for stolen or reused passwords instead.
ftp: FTP (port 21) is an old file-transfer protocol. It sends passwords in plain text.
Forgotten FTP servers full of old backups are a classic weak spot.
passwords: Password reuse means one leak opens many doors: if a password leaks from one system, attackers try it everywhere else.
Defenses: a unique password per system, a password manager, and multi-factor authentication.
trace: In the game, a trace is the target's security noticing you. In real life it's an intrusion detection system (IDS) raising an alert.
Real attackers try to stay quiet; defenders try to shorten the time before they're noticed.
logs: Servers write logs: timestamped lines recording what happened, like logins.
Defenders (the blue team) search logs for patterns, such as many failed logins from one IP followed by a success. That pattern is a brute-force attack.
bruteforce: A brute-force attack tries many passwords until one works.
It leaves a loud trail of failed logins in the logs. Lockouts and rate limits stop it.

missions.title: Hello, World
missions.subject: Welcome to Entropy
body: Entropy takes on authorized security jobs. Before you get real work, show me you can drive a terminal.
1. Run 'scan' to find machines on the network.
missions.hint: Type 'scan', then 'connect 10.0.0.5'. Use 'ls' and 'cd home' to find the files.

lines: If you can read this, you're in.
Now download welcome.txt.
Nice work. Tutorial complete.
Check your mail for your first real job.

missions.title: Credential Reuse
missions.subject: Job: Kestrel Logistics pentest
body: Kestrel Logistics hired us to test their security. You have written permission.
Goal: prove you can get into kestrel-ssh (10.0.2.10) by downloading /root/flag.txt.
Their SSH is hardened, so cracking it won't work. Look for another way in.
Rumor says their old backup server is still online.
Careful: kestrel-ssh will trace you. Plan before you connect.
missions.hint: Crack the FTP port on old-backup, read its files, then use 'login' on kestrel-ssh.

lines: # kestrel admin creds - DO NOT SHARE
svc_backup  Summer2019!
jmorgan     Kestrel#2024
Reminder: James uses the same password everywhere. Fix this!
- IT
FLAG{reused_passwords_are_open_doors}

missions.title: Log Detective
missions.subject: URGENT: someone got into our shop server
body: Hi, we're Harbor Coffee. bit said you could help.
Our admin account was used at 03:12 last night, and none of us did it.
You have access to shop-web (172.16.4.20). The login log is /var/log/auth.log.
Find the attacker's IP and 'report' it so we can block it.
missions.hint: Try 'grep Failed /var/log/auth.log'. Which IP shows up again and again?
